analysis.title: RBC European Rates & Economics Daily (November 4, 2026)
key_insights: US midterms delivered a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate, read as a constraint on President Trump's deregulation and AI-spending agenda. Democrats won the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in 94 years and the Texas Governorship on a message of pushing back on data centre construction.
Trump told the NYT he would accept the election results and work with Democrats.
Treasury yields fell 3-5 bps across the curve because the Democratic result reduced deficit-expansion expectations. The dollar weakened against all G10 peers.
Nasdaq 100 futures were down as much as 2.4% overnight but largely recovered as dip buyers emerged. Dow futures turned positive by early morning.

ECB speakers are increasingly backing a December rate hike. Bundesbank's Nagel and Austria's Kocher said a move is likely if conditions hold, and Radev said the October pause was not the end of tightening.
RBC expects euro area flash HICP inflation unchanged at 3.8% y/y in October. Country data (big upside surprise in Italy, big downside surprise in Germany) suggest modest upside risks to the forecast.

Fuel is expected to subtract from the m/m euro area inflation print despite higher crude, because of tighter petrol-crude spreads and fuel tax cuts. Services inflation is expected to ease to 3.1% y/y from 3.2% on base effects.

RBC expects euro area headline inflation to rise into year-end and peak at 4% in December, on delayed gas price passthrough and some second-round effects. Second-round effects have so far been elusive, so this pressure may not materialise.
RBC does not expect a significant revision to the final UK services PMI from the flash reading of 53.1, the highest since February, nor to the euro area composite PMI.

US rate strategists expect the Treasury refunding announcement to hold auction sizes steady across the curve, with increases starting at the May 2027 QRA, concentrated in 2s/3s/5s. The debt limit may push increases later in the year.

Treasury may be able to remove the 'next several quarters' guidance with minimal impact. Bill supply is set to decline modestly into year-end and the debt limit returns to focus next year. Long-end buybacks are likely to stay at current sizes, no TGA repo announcement is expected, and Treasury should consider moving ahead with SOFR-FRNs.
Consensus expects US services ISM at 54.8 in October versus 54.9 in September.
New Zealand's unemployment rate rose to 5.7%, an 11-year high, days before the national election.
RBC yield forecasts (as of Nov 3): US 10y at 4.91% heading to 5.40% in Q4 2026, US 30y at 5.28% heading to 5.85%, Fed funds midpoint 3.88% heading to 4.13% in Q4 2026 and 4.38% in Q1 2027.
RBC forecasts the ECB deposit rate rising from 2.50% to 2.75% in Q4 2026. It forecasts the BoE rate rising from 3.75% to 4.00% in Q4 2026. The 10y Bund is at 3.31% and the 10y Gilt at 5.23%.

Debt limit timing could delay expected US Treasury auction size increases.
Second-round inflation effects may or may not appear in the euro area.
Democratic control of Congress could constrain Trump's deregulation and AI-spending agenda.
